demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette: The rain had been coming down in sheets the night Leilani’s younger brother, Mateo, lost control of his sedan on the interstate. She was a forensic analyst by trade, trained to objectify evidence and maintain clinical distance, but when dispatch called her to the preliminary scene before the official investigation team arrived, that detachment vanished. She found the car wedged against a concrete barrier, the driver’s side door twisted open like a rip in canvas. The moment her flashlight beam caught Mateo’s glassy eyes, time fractured into a few frozen snapshots in her mind: the shattered dashboard, his outstretched hand brushing the cracked window, the sudden, absolute stillness of his chest. When she finally pulled herself away, the world felt fundamentally untrustworthy. She had come to believe that life was a fragile illusion, that higher powers or human safety nets were entirely absent, and that her own life had been irrevocably destroyed the moment Mateo stopped breathing. Nothing in her marriage or her career felt meaningful anymore; the foundation of her existence had simply cracked. That conviction of ruin quickly shaped her daily rhythms. Convinced that her life was already shattered and stripped of purpose, Leilani found herself unable to summon the will to return to the secure forensic laboratory. The thought of going to work felt like an insult to the permanence of his absence, so she began calling in sick, telling her supervisor her eyes were too strained to examine microslides. Her days bled into a quiet, undereating routine; she would avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, telling herself that hunger was a small, controllable price for enduring the grief. To outrun the silence of her empty apartment, she delayed sleep, staying up until very late, scrolling through work emails she knew she couldn’t process or listening to the hum of the refrigerator, anything to keep the daylight from reminding her of the months slipping by without Mateo. The avoidance of work meant she stopped attending the Tuesday evidence reviews, but the real retreat happened when her car pulled into the garage, turning away from the security checkpoint she once walked through with quiet pride. The very habits she adopted to numb the pain, however, only carved deeper channels for the trauma to return. By delaying sleep and avoiding work, Leilani left herself unstructured and emotionally depleted, which meant the memories no longer needed a direct trigger to surface. When the quiet hours finally pressed in or she sat alone at her kitchen table, she sometimes hears in her head the exact sounds she heard during the frightening event—a phantom screech of tires, the wet slap of rain on the hood, Mateo’s final exhale. She remembers the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment remains a picture in her mind, sharp and unchanging. When the memory returns, she feels so overwhelmed by emotion that she has to stop, pressing her palms against her eyes until her breath steadies. Ironically, this cycle of avoidance and exhaustion convinced her further that her life was destroyed, as her isolation at home and the physical toll of undereating only deepened her conviction that nothing in life felt meaningful anymore. The lost faith she carried was no longer just a philosophical resignation; it was a daily confirmation that she was broken beyond repair. Her negative appraisals continued to act as a lens, magnifying every intrusive memory until it felt like proof of her shattered reality. Because she believed life had been stripped of meaning and her faith in people or a higher power was gone, her mind kept circling back to the wreckage, searching for a logic that would never come. Each time the memory returned and overwhelmed her, she would retreat further, reinforcing the belief that her world was irreparably broken. Now, at the kitchen table with a cold cup of tea she wouldn’t finish, Leilani finally recognized the suffocating architecture of her own coping. The calls to the clinic came not from a sudden shift in grief, but from the quiet terror that if she didn’t confront the loop now, she would never leave her own apartment again. She was most afraid that the wreckage she carried inside had become her only home, and what she hoped for was simply a way to remember Mateo without the memory feeling like a second death.
